tagline.text: A national cultural treasure at Monumento Circle honoring the leader of the Katipunan

location.label: Location
location.text: Monumento Circle, Caloocan (junction of EDSA, MacArthur Highway and Rizal Avenue Extension)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (per person, including transport and a simple meal; the monument itself is free to see)

children.text: This roughly 13.7 m monument stands at Monumento Circle in southern Caloocan and was designed by National Artist Guillermo Tolentino. It honors Andrés Bonifacio, who led the Katipunan, and is right next to LRT-1 Monumento station.
Locals simply call the Bonifacio Monument
Monumento

. It stands in the middle of a large roundabout in southern Caloocan, in northern Metro Manila, where EDSA, MacArthur Highway, Samson Road and Rizal Avenue Extension meet. The name has come to cover the whole neighborhood, and the area is also a key transport hub for traveling in and out of northern Manila. So think of it less as a destination in itself and more as a handy history stop when you are passing through north Manila.

The monument was built to honor Andrés Bonifacio, founder and leader (Supremo) of the Katipunan, which rose against Spanish colonial rule. His call to arms, known as the Cry of Pugad Lawin, is dated to August 23, 1896 (some sources call it the Cry of Balintawak). National Artist Guillermo Tolentino designed it, and construction was ordered during the term of the American governor-general Frank Murphy. The cornerstone was laid on
November 30, 1929
, Bonifacio's 66th birth anniversary, by Aurora Quezon, wife of Senate President Manuel L. Quezon, and the monument was inaugurated on
November 30, 1933
by House Speaker Quintín Paredes. The contract is said to have been worth
The monument is an obelisk

tall. It is made of five parts representing five aspects of society and is crowned by a winged figure symbolizing triumph. Around an octagonal base stand some twenty bronze figures. The octagon stands for the eight provinces that rose against Spain and the eight rays of the Katipunan flag, and the three-step base is said to represent three centuries of Spanish rule. The central figure holds a bolo (a large knife) in one hand and a gun in the other, with an unfurled Katipunan flag shown behind. Pools of water surround the monument.
It was declared a National Historical Landmark on
August 14, 2002
and a National Cultural Treasure on
November 30, 2009

. To be honest, though, this is not a quiet heritage park but a roundabout in the middle of a busy city, packed with cars and people. It suits a short visit for a few photos and some history rather than a leisurely stroll, and it pairs well with nearby Caloocan Cathedral or other northern Manila plans.

The monument was designed by Philippine National Artist Guillermo Tolentino. You take in the five-part obelisk, the winged figure of triumph on top and the group of bronze figures around it in one view. Up close, the expression and gesture of each figure show that this is more than a plain column.

blocks.title: The central figure with a bolo and a gun

children.text: At the heart of the monument stands a figure holding a bolo in one hand and a gun in the other, with an unfurled Katipunan flag behind. These two tools sum up the character of the revolution, so look at this part first.

The octagonal base is explained as the eight provinces that rose against Spain and the eight rays of the Katipunan flag, and the three-step base as three centuries of Spanish rule. The monument rewards what you know, so it is far more fun to walk around once you know what the numbers mean.
It was declared a National Historical Landmark in
and a National Cultural Treasure in
. Recognized at national level as worth preserving, it is considered one of the leading historic sights of northern Manila.

The roundabout in front of the monument is where EDSA, MacArthur Highway, Samson Road and Rizal Avenue Extension meet. LRT-1 Monumento station is close by, so it is easy to come by train from central Manila, and bus and jeepney routes converge around the circle.
The site is known for commemorative events on Bonifacio Day, Bonifacio's birthday,
November 30

. In 2013 the 150th anniversary of Bonifacio's birth and the 80th anniversary of the monument's unveiling were marked on the same date. If you visit that day you may see ceremonies and wreath-laying, but check the schedule beforehand.

items.title: 1–2 hour route
items.subtitle: A loop around the monument from Monumento station

children.text: Get off at LRT-1 Monumento station. The station is close to Monumento Circle, so walk along the road toward the monument. Early in the morning it is cooler and less crowded, which makes it a good time to look around.

Start by viewing the whole monument from the edge of the circle. Look at the obelisk, the winged figure on top and the group of bronze figures below from a distance, then move closer to study their expressions and gestures.

Read the symbols one by one and take photos: the central figure with the bolo and gun, the octagonal base and the three-step structure. The circle is full of traffic, so use the signals and sidewalks when crossing.
Have a simple brunch on the surrounding streets. Several budget eateries in the Grace Park area are well known.
If you have time, head to a nearby sight such as Caloocan Cathedral, or return to central Manila on LRT-1.
Rather than lingering alone, we recommend a short daytime visit and then moving on.
From central Manila (Ermita or the Rizal Avenue side), take LRT-1 north and get off at Monumento station (GL03). The station lies between 5th Avenue and Balintawak on the LRT-1 line.
Wikivoyage notes that Monumento station can be very crowded, with a long queue to buy tickets. Avoiding rush hour makes it much easier.
LRT-1 operating hours and fares can change, so check the operator's latest announcements.

items.title: By bus or jeepney from Manila

children.text: The EDSA Busway (EDSA Carousel) has a Monumento stop, and city bus routes run along MacArthur Highway, Rizal Avenue and C-4 Road.
Many jeepney routes come to Monumento along Rizal Avenue. Check that the destination sign says Monumento, and confirm the fare locally.
Provincial bus terminals such as Victory Liner are near Monumento, so some travelers stop by on the way to northern Luzon.
The usual way is to take a taxi or ride-hailing car from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) into the city and transfer to LRT-1, but road conditions change often, so check travel times locally.
The monument is close to Monumento station and can be reached on foot.
For nearby Caloocan Cathedral or the Grace Park area, take a tricycle or jeepney. Agree on the fare beforehand.

The monument is outdoors in the middle of a roundabout with no admission hours, so you can see it year-round. Some guides recommend visiting between 06:00 and 18:00. After dark visibility is poor and the area is crowded, so a daytime visit is better.

To avoid the heat, the cooler dry season from November to February is best, and in the rainy season from June to November bring an umbrella for showers. Commemorative events are said to be held on Bonifacio Day (November 30) and Independence Day (June 12), so those dates are worth aiming for if your schedule fits.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The best time for photos, and it includes the November 30 anniversary.
Avoid midday and look around early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
Showers and flooding are possible, so bring an umbrella and allow extra time.

There are a few relatively cheap hotels around Monumento. Wikivoyage lists Kabayan Hotel Monumento on MacArthur Highway (76 air-conditioned rooms, from ₱1,075), Chill Hotel Monumento on General Pio Valenzuela Street, and Hotel Sogo on the 5th floor of LRT Northmall on Rizal Avenue Extension. Rates and operations change often, so check the latest information on a booking site.

You can eat at budget eateries around Grace Park. Wikivoyage lists Perry's Chicken House, Tapa ni Mama, Tony's Eatery, Tapsilogan ni Mama Leng and Amber's Food as budget options. Prices depend on the menu and opening hours may change, so check locally. Shopping malls such as SM City Grand Central around the circle and station are also good places to rest when it is hot.
The monument does not take long to see, so fit it briefly into a trip through northern Manila.
Visit in daylight; early morning is the most comfortable.
The circle has very heavy traffic. Use crosswalks and signals, and do not step into the road to take photos.
LRT-1 Monumento station can be crowded, so avoid rush hour and have your ticket or card ready.
On Bonifacio Day (November 30) and Independence Day (June 12), events may cause crowds or traffic controls nearby, so check the latest news beforehand.
Keep your phone and wallet in front and carry your bag on the front of your body. It is also a good habit to watch your surroundings while taking photos.
Knowing the symbolism of the monument (the octagon, the three-step base and the five parts) in advance makes the visit much richer.
This is a crowded roundabout in the middle of a big city, so watch for pickpockets and traffic and keep your visit short, ideally in daylight.
Wikivoyage warns that northern Caloocan has many slums and that illegal drugs and petty crime are concerns. Avoid obviously run-down areas, especially when alone.
Guidance says women should not walk alone and should be especially careful near run-down areas. Go with a companion if possible.
It is noted that revealing clothing such as skimpy shorts in public places can lead to a fine. Dress modestly.
Traffic is extremely complicated, so always check signals and sidewalks when crossing roads.
Opening hours, events and traffic controls can change. Check the Caloocan city tourism information or the latest announcements.
The seat of the Diocese of Caloocan and a historic sight close to Monumento. Check the transport options and travel time locally.

A park that is a good stop on the way back toward central Manila. Travel time varies a lot with traffic.
